title: {{NAME}} and the Last Light of the Mechlight Mountains
moral: What makes a guardian great is not the power to destroy threats, but the wisdom to know which ones need healing instead.

pages.content:
The Mechlight Mountains were, for most of the year, invisible. They generated a field of light-bending shimmer that redirected the eye of any casual observer, but on the equinox, when something shifted in the magnetic frequencies of the peaks, the shimmer thinned, and for three days the mountains were visible as what they were: enormous and ancient, their peaks tipped with towers, their slopes honeycombed with passages that glowed faintly blue from within.

{{NAME}} had been waiting for the equinox for a year, ever since the glimpse of the mountains he had caught the previous spring while on the hillside behind his school, that three-second window of visible impossible peaks before the shimmer closed again.

This time he had been ready. He had walked toward them the moment they appeared.

The mountains grew larger with distance in the wrong direction, the way very important things sometimes do, and by the time {{NAME}} reached the base of the nearest peak he was smaller than he had felt since he was very young.

A superhero was already there, seated on a boulder at the mountain's foot, their armour the warm crimson of brickwork, their helmet off. Her name was Bray, and she was eating an apple with the patient composure of someone waiting for something she knew would take a while.

'You saw them last year too,' {{NAME}} said.

'I've seen them six equinoxes running,' Bray said, and held out an apple she had apparently been keeping for company. 'Come and sit down. I'll explain.'

pages.content:
The mountains had been built, Bray explained, a very long time ago, by a civilisation that was now gone but that had been extraordinarily good at two things: robots and architecture.

The robots they had built were distributed throughout the mountain passages, still running, maintained by their own internal systems, performing the function they had been designed for, which was guarding.

What they were guarding was the unicorn herd that had made its home in the mountain's interior valleys, a herd of several hundred that had found the mountains' warmth and safety and stayed, generation after generation, until the mountain and the herd had become part of the same ecosystem, the robots regulating temperature and air and light within the peaks to suit the unicorns' needs.

'The robots were designed to guard against external threats,' Bray said. 'And they have done that brilliantly for a very long time.'

'But?' {{NAME}} said.

'But one of the guardian robots has developed a fault. A sensor error. It has begun to classify the unicorns themselves as the threat it was designed to guard against. It has started herding them toward the lower passages rather than the safe interior valleys. The unicorns are confused and stressed, the other robots are trying to compensate, and the whole system is beginning to fracture.'

{{NAME}} looked at the blue-glowing passages in the mountain above them. 'Can't you just go in and stop it?'

Bray looked at her apple. 'I tried. The guardian robots don't recognise me as an authorised presence. I made things worse.' She paused. 'I'm good at stopping things. This needs something different.'

pages.content:
The mountain passages were extraordinary, lit by strips of faintly luminescent blue crystal set into the stone, wide enough for a unicorn to walk comfortably, warm with the deep residual heat of whatever powered the ancient systems.

Bray could not come. The guardian robots had catalogued her power signature and treated her as a hazard. But they had not catalogued {{NAME}}, who had never been here before and registered as exactly what he was: a small human child, no apparent threat profile, and therefore someone the guardian robots allowed to pass with the distracted courtesy of very busy security systems.

The fault-robot was in the third deep passage, a sentinel the size of a doorway, its chassis the same blue-crystal colour as the walls, moving in agitated repetitive patterns along the corridor where a group of twenty unicorns had been herded and were now standing with the tense stillness of animals that have nowhere safe to go.

The lead unicorn, silver-white with a horn like spun moonlight, met {{NAME}}'s eyes from across the passage. Her name was somewhere in the mountain air, instinctive: Sola. She was not afraid. She was waiting. As if she too had been expecting someone different from the crimson-armoured figure the robots had rejected.

{{NAME}} sat down in the passage, cross-legged, in the direct sightline of the fault-robot.

The robot stopped its pattern. Its sensors focused on him.

{{NAME}} did not move.

pages.content:
The fault-robot stood over {{NAME}} for a very long minute, its sensor-eyes cycling through multiple classifications, none of which appeared to produce a satisfactory answer.

{{NAME}} waited. He was reasonably certain that what the robot was experiencing was something like confusion, and that confused systems, in his experience, did one of two things: they escalated or they paused. He was counting on the pause.

The pause happened.

While the robot paused, {{NAME}} did something slow and deliberate. He reached into the bag he had brought and withdrew the thing Bray had given him before he entered, a small crystalline diagnostic chip from the original mountain builders' archive that she had spent three equinoxes locating. He held it up so the fault-robot could see it.

The robot's sensors flashed the specific shade of recognition that, according to Bray, the older guardians used for authorised maintenance signals.

{{NAME}} walked forward. The robot stayed still. He found the maintenance panel in its left flank, the one Bray had described from memory with absolute precision, and placed the chip against it.

The robot's chassis vibrated. Its sensor-eyes dimmed and re-lit at a different, steadier frequency.

Then it turned away from the herded unicorns.

And began, slowly and with great purpose, to walk back toward its original position in the deep guardian array.

Sola crossed the passage in four strides and stood before {{NAME}}, her moonlight horn centimetres from his chest, her ancient eyes warm and entirely level.

pages.content:
The mountain settled.

It did so quietly and gradually, the way good things resolve: not with fanfare but with the deep exhale of systems returning to their intended function. The unicorn herd dispersed back into the interior valleys, moving through the blue-lit passages with the ease of creatures who know exactly where home is and have been temporarily, frustratingly, redirected away from it.

Sola walked with {{NAME}} back to the mountain entrance, which was a considerable distance and took some time, and during that time {{NAME}} found, unexpectedly, that walking beside a unicorn in a mountain full of blue crystal light was one of the most peaceful experiences he had ever had.

Bray was where he had left her, or close enough. She had eaten both apples.

'It worked,' she said. Not a question.

'It worked,' {{NAME}} confirmed.

Bray looked at Sola, who stood at the mountain entrance with the composure of a creature that does not require anything from this moment except to be present in it. Bray reached out and touched Sola's mane, very briefly, with the careful reverence of someone who does not do gentle things often and takes the ones they do with great seriousness.

They left the mountain as the equinox shimmer began to return, the peaks receding into their protective invisibility.

{{NAME}} slept that night with the blue-crystal warmth still in his memory, and woke before dawn reaching for the diagnostic chip that was no longer there, and lay still for a moment in the specific happy sadness of remembering that something wonderful was already over and also not over at all, because next equinox was three hundred and sixty-four days away and already he was counting.
